extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate students and researchers in combinatorics and discrete geometry
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of proof techniques and methodological ingredients used to produce and analyse combinatorial-geometry and graph-theory results (e.g., Graham–Pollak theorem, the slope problem, Euler applications, Cauchy rigidity, Pick's formula, touching simplices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear-algebra translation for decompositions (Graham–Pollak style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate a graph-decomposition statement into algebraic relations by associating a variable to each vertex and expressing edge-relationships as polynomial/linear equations; then use linear-algebraic dimension/nullspace arguments to reach a contradiction or bound (e.g., assign variables xi to vertices, derive equation (1), observe fewer equations than variables ⇒ non-trivial solution ⇒ contradiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps illustrated: associate a variable xi to every vertex; express that Hj decompose Kn as an identity (equation (1)); assume contrary (m < n−1) to get a linear system with fewer equations than variables; obtain nontrivial solution and deduce pairwise products vanish (cicj = 0), leading to a contradiction via sum-of-squares. Note: authors stress there is no purely combinatorial proof known for this result — linear algebra is the standard approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce to a simpler parity/case (even/odd) before attacking (slope problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving a lower bound on the number of slopes determined by n points, reduce to an easier canonical parity case (here: it suffices to show the statement for even n = 2m because odd n can be handled by removing one point).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use trivial base cases (n=3) and the observation that any set of 2m+1 non-collinear points contains a 2m-subset not all on a line; prove the even case and lift to odd n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model planar direction changes by a periodic sequence of permutations
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace geometric motion of projection direction by a sequence of permutations π0 → π1 → … → πt capturing point orderings; encode slopes as permutation-change events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties required of the model: π0 = 123...n, πt = n...321, length t equals number of slopes, every pair i<j is switched exactly once, and every move reverses one or more disjoint increasing substrings. Constructing such a periodic sequence reduces geometric slope questions to combinatorial constraints on permutations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Barrier-counting: split permutations into left/right halves and count crossings
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide each permutation into left and right halves (equal size m = n/2) and count letters that cross the central barrier to obtain lower bounds (sum over crossing moves of 2·di ≥ n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define a crossing move of order d as reversal moving 2d letters across the barrier. Each letter must cross at least once during π0→πt, giving ∑ 2di ≥ n. This counting is a key quantitative ingredient in proving t ≥ n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify permutation moves as crossing, touching, or ordinary
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorize each reversal move in the permutation sequence: crossing (involves letters from both sides of barrier), touching (reversal adjacent to barrier but not crossing), ordinary (neither touching nor crossing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric interpretations: crossing = direction of a line with < m points on each side; touching = line with exactly m points on one side (hence at most m−2 on the other); ordinary = other lines. Use this classification to structure the combinatorial counting argument (T, C(d), O pattern).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local pattern constraints between move types (T-O-C inequalities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit structural constraints among the three move types: (i) between any two crossing moves there is at least one touching move; (ii) between a crossing move of order d and the next touching move there are at least d−1 ordinary moves; and the symmetric statement between touching then crossing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These facts follow from how decreasing/increasing substrings evolve under moves and imply that a crossing move of order d is embedded into a pattern of length 2d (T followed by ≥d−1 O, then C(d), then ≥d−1 O). Summing such blocks yields the desired global lower bound on t.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual graph + spanning-tree argument for Euler’s formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove n − e + f = 2 for connected plane graphs by picking a spanning tree T, constructing the dual graph G*, and showing the complement edges correspond to a spanning tree T* of the dual; combine counts for trees (vertices = edges+1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct G* by placing a vertex in each face and connecting vertices for shared boundary edges (allow multiple edges). Let T be a spanning tree of G; edges E\,T correspond to edges T* in G* that form a spanning tree because T has no cycle and E\,T cannot induce a cycle in the dual. Then n = eT + 1 and f = eT* + 1, summing yields Euler's formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-counting identities for vertices/edges/faces
rubrics_metrics.description: Use two-way counting to obtain 2e = ∑ i·ni (degrees) and 2e = ∑ k·fk (face-sides), and n = ∑ ni, f = ∑ fk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretations: count edge-vertex incidences to get degree-sum identity; count edge-face incidences to get face-side identity. Derive average degree d = 2e/n and average face-side f¯ = 2e/f. These identities are repeatedly used to deduce numerical inequalities for planar graphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive standard planar-graph inequalities from Euler + counting
rubrics_metrics.description: From Euler and the double-counting identities, deduce classical consequences: (A) e ≤ 3n − 6 for simple plane graphs with n>2; (B) existence of a vertex of degree ≤5; (C) in any 2-coloring of edges, there is a vertex with at most two color-changes around it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketches: (A) every face has ≥3 sides ⇒ 2e ≥ 3f ⇒ combine with Euler to get e ≤ 3n−6. (B) follows from (A) and average degree <6. (C) count corners with color changes and bound via face-side counts to force a vertex with ≤2 changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dualization/projective transform to convert point-line problems to arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: Convert point configurations in the plane to arrangements of great circles on the sphere (or dual objects) so that incidence/line questions become graph/arrangement questions amenable to Euler-type arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Sylvester–Gallai: embed R2 in S2 and replace each point pair ±v by corresponding great circle Cv; then vertices are intersections of great circles giving a plane graph on S2. Apply planar-graph degree/face arguments (via Proposition (B)) to obtain the existence of a vertex of degree 4, yielding the Sylvester–Gallai conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use parity / color-change corner counting for colored arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: In colored arrangements (e.g., two-colored great circles or edges), count sign or color-change corners and apply face/edge counting to deduce existence of monochromatic features or constrained-change vertices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monochromatic lines theorem: after dualization to great circles colored black/white, use Proposition (C) which bounds color-changes around a vertex; counting arguments show some intersection must be incident only to circles of one color, giving a monochromatic line in the primal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangulate lattice polygons and apply Euler to get Pick's theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute area of an integer-vertex polygon by triangulating it into elementary triangles (area 1/2) and using Euler's formula combined with counts of interior/boundary lattice points to derive A(Q) = n_int + 1/2 n_bd − 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key steps: triangulate using all lattice points (interior and boundary); interpret triangulation as a plane graph with f−1 triangles of area 1/2; relate triangle-side counts to interior/boundary edges and vertices, apply Euler, and simplify to Pick's formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edge-signing/angle-comparison method for rigidity (Cauchy)
rubrics_metrics.description: To compare two combinatorially equivalent convex polyhedra with congruent corresponding faces, sign/colour edges by whether the dihedral angle in one exceeds the other, transfer the resulting 2-coloured graph to the sphere, use planar constraints to find a vertex with few sign-changes, then examine local spherical polygons around that vertex to derive contradiction via an arm-lemma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: mark edges as + (larger in P') or − (smaller); radial projection maps the edge-coloured graph to the sphere; part (C) gives a vertex with ≤2 sign-changes; intersect with a small sphere to get spherical polygons Q and Q' with same side-lengths but angle differences; apply Cauchy's arm lemma to conclude the missing edge length must have contradictory inequalities, proving equality of dihedral angles and hence rigidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy’s arm lemma (monotonicity of opposite side length under angle increase)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two convex (planar or spherical) n-gons have corresponding edge lengths equal and each internal angle αi ≤ αi' for i=2..n−1, then the length of the closing edge q1qn is ≤ corresponding length in the primed polygon; equality holds iff all αi = αi'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by induction: base n=3 follows from the cosine law (planar) or spherical trigonometric cosine formula. For n≥4, either cut off a vertex where angles match (induction) or increase an angle as far as possible preserving convexity and use triangle inequalities and inductive comparisons. Lemma is applied to spherical polygons arising from local vertex neighborhoods in the rigidity proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive lower-bound via affine transforms + induction (touching simplices)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show f(d) ≥ 2^d for the maximum number of pairwise touching d-simplices in R^d, give an explicit inductive construction using affine coordinate transformations so that a transversal line hits the interior of every simplex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Zaks's theorem: produce families of 2^d pairwise touching d-simplices with a transversal line intersecting all interiors. The method relies on careful affine-positioning and induction on dimension; the text records the construction idea and states the conjectured exact value f(d)=2^d.
